items.title: Breaking: Zimbabwe Miners Federation Extends President Rushwaya’s Term to 2033
items.summary: The Zimbabwe Miners Federation (ZMF) has voted to extend President Henrietta Rushwaya’s tenure to 2033, a move the organisation says will ensure policy continuity and institutional stability in a sector crucial to the…
items.body:
The Zimbabwe Miners Federation (ZMF) has voted to extend President Henrietta Rushwaya’s tenure to 2033, a move the organisation says will ensure policy continuity and institutional stability in a sector crucial to the nation’s economy. The resolution was ratified during the ZMF’s Special General Council Meeting and Annual General Meeting (AGM). Delegates voted overwhelmingly in favour of the extension, with 180 votes for and just one against. The motion, originally tabled by Mashonaland West Province’s Timothy Chizuzu, extends the presidential and executive term of office from five to seven years. It was seconded by Midlands Chairman Makumba Nyenje, who also successfully moved an amendment to extend the tenure of General Council members to 2033, subject to the necessary constitutional amendments. The ZMF stated that leadership continuity is necessary to consolidate ongoing reforms in the mining sector. The motion specifically cites the need for consistent leadership to drive the transformation of the sector through formalisation, mechanisation, beneficiation, and environmental sustainability. The extended mandate solidifies Rushwaya’s influence over the federation, which represents both large-scale and small-scale miners in a country heavily reliant on mineral exports such as gold and lithium. Policy certainty and stable institutional leadership are frequently cited by international investors as critical factors when deploying capital in emerging markets. items.title: Zimplats Appoints Stanley Segula as CEO, Mhembere Retires After 19 Years
items.summary: Zimplats has appointed Dr Stanley Segula as its new Chief Executive Officer, replacing long-serving CEO Alexander Mhembere, who will retire from the position on 1 November 2026 after 19 years at the helm. The platinum…
items.body:
Zimplats has appointed Dr Stanley Segula as its new Chief Executive Officer, replacing long-serving CEO Alexander Mhembere, who will retire from the position on 1 November 2026 after 19 years at the helm. The platinum producer announced on Friday that Segula’s appointment follows a structured succession process, with Mhembere stepping down as CEO and executive director but retaining his position as Chairman of Zimbabwe Platinum Mines (Private) Limited. Segula brings more than 30 years of experience across the mining value chain. He joined the Implats Group in April 2008 and has served as Managing Director of Zimbabwe Platinum Mines since November 2015. He has played a key role in advancing mechanisation, innovation and operational efficiency at the company. His qualifications include a PhD in Strategic Management and Leadership, an MBA and a Bachelor of Science Honours degree in Mining Engineering. Mhembere leaves after nearly two decades during which Zimplats expanded its underground mining operations, processing capacity and renewable energy investments, while strengthening its contribution to Zimbabwe’s mining and beneficiation ambitions. Trending Strategic Minerals Price Index – 9 March 2026 Zimplats Chairman Professor Sydney Mufamadi said Segula’s appointment reflected the depth of leadership talent within the company and expressed confidence in his ability to steer its next phase of growth. Segula said his immediate priorities would be to maintain workplace safety, improve operational performance and ensure disciplined investment. The company said the leadership transition would be supported by a structured handover to maintain continuity in its strategy and stakeholder relationships. Linkedin Facebook X WhatsApp Email

items.title: Hwange Colliery to Host Mine Rescue Competitions 2026
items.summary: Preparations are complete for the Mine Rescue National Competitions , scheduled for 30 October 2026 at Hwange Colliery’s Hwange 3 Main North, bringing together mining teams from across the country to demonstrate their…
items.body:
Preparations are complete for the Mine Rescue National Competitions , scheduled for 30 October 2026 at Hwange Colliery’s Hwange 3 Main North, bringing together mining teams from across the country to demonstrate their preparedness, technical expertise and teamwork, Mining Zimbabwe can report. The event is being organised by the Chamber of Mines of Zimbabwe (CoMZ) in partnership with HCCL Holdings under the theme “Kamandama Drives Our Commitment. Prepared, Equipped, Ready to Save Lives.” The competitions will provide a platform for participating teams to demonstrate their emergency response capabilities, technical proficiency, discipline and ability to work under pressure. Through practical demonstrations and rescue exercises, the teams will showcase the skills and coordination required to respond effectively to mining emergencies. A total of five teams will compete in the non-donning category: Zimplats SMC, Jena Mines, Blanket Mine, Shamva Gold and Pan African Mine. The donning category will feature seven teams, namely Blanket Mine, Mimosa Mine, Zimplats Mine, Howmine, Redwing Mine, Freda Rebecca Mine and the host team, Hwange Colliery Mine. Beyond the competitive aspect, the event will provide an opportunity for teams to exchange knowledge, sharpen their skills and strengthen collaboration in emergency response. It also highlights the mining sector’s commitment to maintaining high safety standards and improving rescue preparedness. items.title: Mine Managers gear up for the 2026 AGM, Conference & technical visit
items.summary: The Association of Mine Managers of Zimbabwe (AMMZ) will hold its 2026 Annual General Meeting (AGM), Conference and Technical Visit from 1 to 4 November at Troutbeck Resort in Nyanga, bringing together mining…
items.body:
The Association of Mine Managers of Zimbabwe (AMMZ) will hold its 2026 Annual General Meeting (AGM), Conference and Technical Visit from 1 to 4 November at Troutbeck Resort in Nyanga, bringing together mining professionals for discussions, networking and technical engagement. The four-day event will include conference sessions, a golf tournament or social excursion, and a technical visit to the Zimbabwe Consolidated Diamond Company (ZCDC) on 4 November. The technical visit to ZCDC on 4 November will provide participants with an opportunity to engage with the diamond mining operation. Delegates wishing to attend must provide their national identification numbers for security pre-clearance. Organisers have also made bus transport available from Mutare, departing at 0900 hours for early registrants. Latecomers will be required to travel individually. Registration fees are payable to the Chamber of Mines of Zimbabwe at its Accounts Office, 20 Mt Pleasant Drive, Mt Pleasant, Harare, or through a bank deposit into the organisation’s account. Invoices and banking details can be obtained by contacting [email protected] . Trending ‘Money Is There, but Miners Can’t See It’: Mnangagwa Offers Local Financing Key The conference provides a platform for mine managers and other industry professionals to exchange knowledge, strengthen professional networks and engage with technical developments relevant to Zimbabwe’s mining sector. The event will conclude with the technical visit to ZCDC on 4 November. items.title: One-on-One with Sandvik Auto Electrician Progress Marikano
items.summary: Rebuilding heavy mining equipment requires precision, technical skill, and deep mechanical understanding. Since joining Sandvik as an apprentice in 2012 and qualifying as a Class 1 Millwright in 2016, this specialised…
items.body:
Rebuilding heavy mining equipment requires precision, technical skill, and deep mechanical understanding. Since joining Sandvik as an apprentice in 2012 and qualifying as a Class 1 Millwright in 2016, this specialised auto-electrician has built a career restoring complex machines such as load haul dumpers (LHDs), dump trucks, and drill rigs at the company’s Harare workshop. In this interview, Progress Marikano shares insights into the process of rebuilding mining machinery and reflects on her journey in the trades while balancing a demanding technical career with family life as a wife and mother. Progress, your journey from a 2012 apprentice to a specialised auto-electrician is impressive. What made you choose a trade like this, and what was the most important lesson you learned during those four years of training that still guides your work today? I have always been fascinated by how complex systems work together to form a unit. Before my apprenticeship, I was a medical student, but when I could not finish the course, I saw being a millwright as very similar to medicine. Both investigate symptoms, run tests, rule out possibilities, and identify root causes. They both rely on observation, logic, and experience. You take something broken and make it whole again. They are different trades, yet almost identical. Trending ‘Money Is There, but Miners Can’t See It’: Mnangagwa Offers Local Financing Key A millwright is a jack of all trades. During training, you gain skills in automotive engineering, electrical, mechanical fitting, welding, hydraulics, and fitting and turning. The most important lesson I learnt is to look at a machine as a whole. The electrical does not work separately, and the hydraulic does not work separately. They work together towards a common cause; it is…

items.title: Stanbic Bank’s Tania Mandaza on Mining Finance, Bankability and Africa’s Rare Earth Future
items.summary: Tania Mandaza, Vice President for Mining & Metals at Stanbic Bank, sits at the intersection of finance and mining, where she helps shape how African mining projects are structured and funded. In this interview, she…
items.body:
Tania Mandaza, Vice President for Mining & Metals at Stanbic Bank, sits at the intersection of finance and mining, where she helps shape how African mining projects are structured and funded. In this interview, she shares insights on bankability, risk assessment, and why Zimbabwe must shift from raw mineral exports to value-added industrialisation. Tania, your role as Vice President for Mining & Metals at Stanbic Bank places you at the nexus of finance and mining. What was your path to this specialised field? Was it a planned focus, and what initially drew you to the mining sector from a banking perspective? Well, my path wasn’t a straight line from Finance into Mining, and it certainly wasn’t a planned focus. I have built a solid foundation in finance through studies in Accounting, Marketing and an MBA in Strategic Leadership, complemented by a specialised program at the Gordon Institute of Business Science in South Africa, which further strengthened my financial expertise. About 10 years ago, an unexpected opportunity arose within Client Coverage-what other banks call Corporate Banking-to join the Mining Finance Portfolio. At the time, I was managing Non-Bank Financial Institutions(NBFI) and Consumer Agriculture clients. My experience with NBFIs gave me a strong foundation in structuring complex deals, managing diverse risks, and working with global stakeholders. Those skills proved invaluable when I transitioned into mining finance, where projects are equally complex, capital-intensive, and require innovative solutions to balance risk and reward. Agriculture, on the other hand, is life-sustaining and cyclical, tied to natural renewal and human consumption. Mining, by contrast, is finite and extractive, focused on unlocking hidden resources that cannot be replenished.…

items.title: Muriel Mine’s Dump Retreatment Drives Output 425% as Exploration Extends Life of Mine
items.summary: Pan African’s Muriel Mine has more than quadrupled gold production over two years through an intensive dump retreatment operation, while a sustained exploration campaign has extended the underground life of mine to five…
items.body:
Pan African’s Muriel Mine has more than quadrupled gold production over two years through an intensive dump retreatment operation, while a sustained exploration campaign has extended the underground life of mine to five years, according to figures presented during a technical visit by the Association of Mine Managers of Zimbabwe (AMMZ) . By Rudairo Mapuranga Production climbed from 3,600 ounces (approximately 120 kilograms) in 2023 to 15,000 ounces (425 kilograms) in 2024, reaching 20,000 ounces (630 kilograms) in 2025, management reported to visiting industry peers. The surge was driven entirely by hydrosluicing of historical tailings—a distinction mine officials emphasised during the AMMZ tour. Underground ore from newly delineated resources is not yet being processed; a crusher is currently under construction to handle the harder primary material once the dump is exhausted. Cash costs per ounce held steady at roughly US$1,000 in 2023, US$1,021 in 2024, and US$1,004 in 2025, demonstrating operational efficiency despite inflationary pressures across Zimbabwe’s mining sector. Trending ‘Money Is There, but Miners Can’t See It’: Mnangagwa Offers Local Financing Key The production turnaround follows a sustained exploration campaign that has extended Muriel’s underground mine life to approximately five years, according to figures presented at the technical visit. This contrasts sharply with the operation’s historical struggles: a 2015 assessment showed Muriel required ore grades of 4 to 5 grams per tonne to remain viable but was mining at around 2.5 grams per tonne in the absence of new exploration and development. However, the underground resources that provide this extended life are not yet being mined. The operation is currently focused on processing the remaining tailin…

items.title: Muriel Mine Hydrosluicing: How a mine in Zimbabwe is Turning Tailings Into Gold
items.summary: Pan African-owned Muriel Mine has turned a legacy tailings storage facility into a profitable production asset through a carefully engineered hydrosluicing and carbon-in-leach process. With the dump now in its final…
items.body:
Pan African-owned Muriel Mine has turned a legacy tailings storage facility into a profitable production asset through a carefully engineered hydrosluicing and carbon-in-leach process. With the dump now in its final five months of life, the operation offers a textbook case of efficient surface mining, water recycling, and integrated processing, all while funding a major exploration drive that has extended the mine’s underground life to five years. The following technical overview, compiled from presentations made during an Association of Mine Managers of Zimbabwe (AMMZ) technical visit, details every stage of the process. Webster Chemhuru, Senior Plant Metallurgist, led the delegation through the hydrosluicing and processing circuits, while specialised contractor BillNick Engineering provided additional insights into the hydrosluicing system and tailings management. Water Sourcing and Storage The hydrosluicing operation relies on a dual-source water supply. Sixty per cent of the water comes from Chawara Dam, located approximately four to five kilometres from the mine and shared with local farmers. The remaining forty per cent is recycled water drawn from the active tailings storage facility. This water is detoxified to break down residual cyanide before reuse, reducing both fresh water consumption and the operation’s environmental footprint. Trending ‘Money Is There, but Miners Can’t See It’: Mnangagwa Offers Local Financing Key Water is first stored in a 10,000-cubic-metre tank. From there, it is fed into a high-pressure system where pumps deliver water to the hydrosluicing monitor at pressures of 1,500 to 1,800 kilopascals at the nozzle. items.title: Inside Kundai Mudzviti’s rise in Zimbabwe’s Gold power circle
items.summary: At just 27, Kundai Mudzviti is redefining what it means to build a career in communications. From excelling as a journalism student at NUST to stepping into academia as an Assistant Lecturer, and now shaping the public…
items.body:
At just 27, Kundai Mudzviti is redefining what it means to build a career in communications. From excelling as a journalism student at NUST to stepping into academia as an Assistant Lecturer, and now shaping the public voice of Fidelity Gold Refinery, her journey is anything but conventional. In this interview, she reflects on an unplanned path into media, the lessons learned from the newsroom, and the realities of managing communications at the heart of Zimbabwe’s gold sector, all while balancing the demands of career, leadership, and motherhood. Kundai, you’re only 27, and you’ve already built a career that spans journalism, academia, and corporate communications. Let’s start at the beginning. What drew you to media and communications in the first place? Was there a specific moment or person that made you say, “This is what I want to do with my life”? To be frank, no one really inspired me. I don’t have that story of a teacher or a mentor who pointed me in this direction. In fact, I wanted to do law. That was the plan. But life happened, and I found myself in journalism instead. Some people say journalists are failed lawyers, and maybe there is some truth to that in my case! But once I arrived in Media, I stayed because I realised I loved the craft. At NUST, I was one of the best students there were only two of us at the top, really, and that excellence opened doors. I became an Assistant Lecturer while still young, and that experience shaped my confidence more than anything else. Suddenly, I was the knowledgeable one in the room. I didn’t have a “Eureka!” moment. I just kept showing up, and the path revealed itself. Law’s loss was communication’s gain.
